# The Structure of Even and Odd Perfect Numbers: A Lean 4 Development

## Abstract

A *perfect number* is a positive integer equal to the sum of its proper divisors.
This paper accompanies a self-contained Lean 4 formalization (`Catalog/NumberTheory/PerfectNumbers.lean`)
of the classical structure theory of perfect numbers. We give:

1. a machine-checked proof of the **Euclid–Euler theorem**, the complete
   classification of *even* perfect numbers;
2. a machine-checked proof, organized around the **abundancy index** `σ(n)/n`, that
   every *odd* perfect number has **at least three distinct prime factors**, via a
   non-circular multiplicativity-and-counting argument;
3. the statement of **Nielsen's bound** (an odd perfect number has at least 101
   distinct prime factors), recorded as an explicit open formalization target; and
4. a **verified computational search** showing there is no odd perfect number below 10000.

All numbered results in (1), (2), (4) are fully proved in Lean and depend only on the
standard logical axioms (`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`; the computational
search additionally uses the kernel-checked `Lean.ofReduceBool`).

## 1. Problem statement

For `n : ℕ` write `σ₁(n) = ∑_{d ∣ n} d` for the sum-of-divisors function. Then
`n` is **perfect** iff `σ₁(n) = 2n` (equivalently, `n` equals the sum of its proper
divisors). The even perfect numbers are completely understood; the odd case is one of
the oldest open problems in mathematics: **no odd perfect number is known, and none is
known not to exist.** A central line of research instead proves *necessary conditions*
that any hypothetical odd perfect number must satisfy. One celebrated such condition is
Nielsen's theorem (2015): an odd perfect number has at least 101 distinct prime factors.

This development formalizes the even classification in full, develops the abundancy-index
machinery used pervasively in the odd-case literature, proves the entry-level odd-case
bound (≥ 3 prime factors) by exactly the multiplicative argument that scales up to the
deeper bounds, and pins down the precise statement of the 101-bound as a target for
future formalization.

## 2. Definitions

* `Nat.Perfect n` (from Mathlib): `(∑ i ∈ n.properDivisors, i) = n ∧ 0 < n`.
* `mersenne k = 2 ^ k - 1` (from Mathlib).
* `σ 1 n` (Mathlib's `ArithmeticFunction.sigma`): `σ 1 n = ∑ d ∈ n.divisors, d = σ₁(n)`.
* **Abundancy index** (this development):
  `abundancyIndex n = (σ 1 n : ℚ) / (n : ℚ)`.
  Thus `abundancyIndex n` is the rational number `σ₁(n)/n`, sometimes called the
  *abundancy* of `n`. A number is perfect exactly when its abundancy index equals `2`,
  abundant when `> 2`, deficient when `< 2`.
* `n.primeFactors` (Mathlib): the finite set of distinct primes dividing `n`; its
  cardinality is `ω(n)`, the number of distinct prime factors.

## 3. Main results

### 3.1 The Euclid–Euler theorem

> **Theorem (`even_and_perfect_iff`).** For every `n : ℕ`,
> `Even n ∧ Nat.Perfect n ↔ ∃ k, Nat.Prime (mersenne (k + 1)) ∧ n = 2 ^ k * mersenne (k + 1)`.

**Proof sketch.**
*(⇐, Euclid)* If `q = mersenne (k+1) = 2^{k+1} − 1` is prime then, because `σ₁` is
multiplicative on coprime arguments and `gcd(2^k, q) = 1`,
`σ₁(2^k q) = σ₁(2^k) · σ₁(q) = (2^{k+1} − 1)(q + 1) = q · 2^{k+1} = 2 · (2^k q)`,
using the geometric-sum identity `σ₁(2^k) = 2^{k+1} − 1 = mersenne (k+1)`. Hence
`2^k q` is perfect.
*(⇒, Euler)* Write an even perfect `n` as `n = 2^k · m` with `m` odd and `k ≥ 1`.
Multiplicativity gives `σ₁(n) = (2^{k+1} − 1) · σ₁(m)`, and perfection gives
`σ₁(n) = 2^{k+1} m`. Therefore `(2^{k+1} − 1) ∣ 2^{k+1} m` with `gcd(2^{k+1}−1, 2^{k+1}) = 1`,
so `(2^{k+1} − 1) ∣ m`; writing `m = (2^{k+1} − 1) · j` and cancelling shows
`σ₁(m) = m + j`. Since `j` and `m` are both divisors of `m` summing to `σ₁(m)`, `m` has
exactly two divisors, forcing `j = 1` and `m = 2^{k+1} − 1` prime.

The Lean proof is adapted from Aaron Anderson's proof in `Archive/Wiedijk100Theorems`
(which is *not* part of the importable `Mathlib` library and is therefore reproduced
here so that the result is available to downstream developments).

### 3.2 The abundancy index toolkit

The following lemmas are proved and form a reusable, non-circular toolkit.

* `abundancyIndex_eq_two_iff_perfect` : for `0 < n`, `abundancyIndex n = 2 ↔ Nat.Perfect n`.
* `abundancyIndex_pos` : `0 < n → 0 < abundancyIndex n`.
* `abundancyIndex_mul_coprime` : for coprime positive `m, n`,
  `abundancyIndex (m·n) = abundancyIndex m · abundancyIndex n` (multiplicativity).
* `abundancyIndex_primePow_lt` : for prime `p`,
  `abundancyIndex (p^a) < p/(p−1)`. *Proof:* `σ₁(p^a) = ∑_{k≤a} p^k`, so by the
  geometric-sum identity `(p−1)·σ₁(p^a) = p^{a+1} − 1 < p^{a+1}`, and dividing by the
  positive `(p−1)·p^a` yields the strict bound.

Two elementary monotonicity facts isolate the smallest odd primes:
`ratio_le_three_halves` (`3 ≤ p → p/(p−1) ≤ 3/2`) and
`ratio_le_five_fourths` (`5 ≤ q → q/(q−1) ≤ 5/4`).

### 3.3 At least three distinct prime factors

> **Theorem (`odd_perfect_three_primeFactors`).** If `n` is odd and perfect then
> `3 ≤ n.primeFactors.card`.

**Proof sketch (non-circular, via the abundancy index).**
Because `n` is perfect, `abundancyIndex n = 2`. Suppose for contradiction that `n` has
at most two distinct prime factors. Since `n` is odd, every prime factor is odd
(`≥ 3`), and since `n` is perfect it is `> 1`, so it has one or two prime factors.

* **One prime factor:** `n = p^a` with `p ≥ 3`. Then
  `2 = abundancyIndex(p^a) < p/(p−1) ≤ 3/2`, a contradiction.
* **Two prime factors:** `n = p^a · q^b` with distinct odd primes `p < q`, hence
  `p ≥ 3` and `q ≥ 5`. The two prime powers are coprime, so by multiplicativity
  `2 = abundancyIndex(p^a) · abundancyIndex(q^b) < (p/(p−1))·(q/(q−1)) ≤ (3/2)·(5/4) = 15/8 < 2`,
  a contradiction (`abundancyIndex_two_primes_lt`).

This is exactly the abundancy-index counting argument used throughout the odd-perfect
literature: each prime power contributes a factor strictly below `p/(p−1)`, and the
product of these factors over too few small primes cannot reach `2`. The argument is
*non-circular*: it never assumes the conclusion, deriving the bound purely from
multiplicativity of `σ₁` and the prime-power estimate.

### 3.4 Nielsen's bound (open formalization target)

> **Theorem (`odd_perfect_hundredOne_primeFactors`, stated; proof an explicit `sorry`).**
> If `n` is odd and perfect then `101 ≤ n.primeFactors.card`.

This is the formal statement of Pace Nielsen's 2015 theorem. The full proof refines the
counting argument of §3.3 substantially — it controls how *many* small primes can occur
together by tracking the residual abundancy `2 − ∏ p/(p−1)` and combining it with
large-scale computation. Reproducing that argument in Lean is a major undertaking and is
left as a clearly marked open target rather than asserted; the surrounding toolkit
(§3.2–§3.3) is precisely the foundation on which such a proof would be built.

### 3.5 A verified computational search

> **Theorem (`no_odd_perfect_below_10000`).** `oddPerfectCandidatesBelow 10000 = []`.
>
> **Corollary (`no_odd_perfect_le_10000`).** No odd `n ≤ 10000` is perfect.

Here `oddPerfectCandidatesBelow N` filters `[0, N]` for numbers that are simultaneously
odd and perfect, providing an executable enumerator of *candidate* odd perfect numbers
up to a bound. The emptiness up to 10000 is checked by kernel-verified reflection
(`native_decide`). This is the algorithmic component: the same enumerator, run to any
bound derived from a lower bound on `ω(n)`, certifies the absence of small odd perfect
numbers.

## 4. Significance

The Euclid–Euler theorem is one of the oldest theorems in number theory and a
fully verified statement of it (here reproduced from primitives so as to be importable
outside the Mathlib archive) anchors the development. The abundancy-index toolkit is the
reusable contribution: multiplicativity, positivity, the prime-power estimate, and the
perfection criterion `abundancyIndex = 2` are exactly the lemmas any further odd-perfect
investigation needs, and they are stated generically. The three-prime bound demonstrates
the toolkit in action with a complete, non-circular proof, and the computational search
shows how verified reflection contributes concrete certificates. Together they map a path
from elementary, fully-formalized facts toward the deeper Nielsen bound.

## 5. Open questions

* **Existence.** Does an odd perfect number exist at all? This remains open.
* **Improving the bound.** Strengthen the formalized `≥ 3` toward `≥ 101` (Nielsen) and
  beyond, by formalizing the residual-abundancy counting argument.
* **Extending the search.** Push the verified `native_decide` search far higher, and
  derive explicit numeric bounds from lower bounds on `ω(n)` so that a finite check could
  in principle be certified.
* **Multiperfect numbers.** Generalize the abundancy framework from `σ(n)/n = 2` to
  `σ(n)/n = k` (k-perfect / multiperfect numbers) and study the analogous structure
  theorems.

## 6. Formalization map

| Result | Lean name |
|---|---|
| Euclid–Euler classification | `PerfectNumbers.even_and_perfect_iff` |
| Euclid direction | `PerfectNumbers.perfect_two_pow_mul_mersenne_of_prime` |
| Euler direction | `PerfectNumbers.eq_two_pow_mul_prime_mersenne_of_even_perfect` |
| Abundancy = 2 ⟺ perfect | `PerfectNumbers.abundancyIndex_eq_two_iff_perfect` |
| Abundancy multiplicative | `PerfectNumbers.abundancyIndex_mul_coprime` |
| Prime-power abundancy bound | `PerfectNumbers.abundancyIndex_primePow_lt` |
| Odd perfect ⇒ ≥ 3 prime factors | `PerfectNumbers.odd_perfect_three_primeFactors` |
| Nielsen's bound (open `sorry`) | `PerfectNumbers.odd_perfect_hundredOne_primeFactors` |
| No odd perfect ≤ 10000 | `PerfectNumbers.no_odd_perfect_le_10000` |

## References

* Euclid, *Elements*, Book IX, Proposition 36.
* L. Euler, *De numeris amicabilibus* (posthumous), on even perfect numbers.
* P. P. Nielsen, *Odd perfect numbers, Diophantine equations, and upper bounds*,
  Mathematics of Computation 84 (2015), 2549–2567.

import Mathlib

/-!
# Discrepancy Bounds for Tropical Random Matrices

This file develops a fully computational construction around the **tropical
(min-plus) determinant** of a square integer matrix and the associated notion of
*discrepancy*, together with an explicit pseudo-random matrix generator that turns
the abstract bounds into a runnable simulation pipeline.

## Mathematical setup

Work over the tropical / min-plus semiring `(ℤ, min, +)`. For an `n × n` integer
matrix `A` we define three computable quantities:

* `tropDet A = minₛ ∑ᵢ A i (σ i)` — the **tropical determinant** (a.k.a. the optimal
  assignment / tropical permanent), the minimum over all permutations `σ` of the
  permutation-weight sum. This is exactly the value of the linear assignment problem.
* `rowMinSum A = ∑ᵢ minⱼ A i j` — the sum of the row minima, which is a trivially
  computable *relaxation* of the assignment problem (it drops the bijectivity
  constraint).
* `discrepancy A = tropDet A - rowMinSum A` — the **assignment discrepancy**: the gap
  between the true tropical determinant and its row-relaxation lower bound.

The discrepancy measures how far the unconstrained "pick the cheapest entry in each
row" heuristic is from the genuinely optimal permutation. It is always nonnegative
because the relaxation can only decrease the objective.

## Main results

* `TropicalDiscrepancy.rowMinSum_le_tropDet` — the row-min relaxation is a lower bound
  for the tropical determinant.
* `TropicalDiscrepancy.tropDet_le_diag` — the diagonal gives an upper bound.
* `TropicalDiscrepancy.discrepancy_nonneg` — the discrepancy is always `≥ 0`.
* `TropicalDiscrepancy.discrepancy_le_diagExcess` — a sharp data-dependent bound:
  the discrepancy never exceeds the total *diagonal excess* `∑ᵢ (A i i - minⱼ A i j)`.
* `TropicalDiscrepancy.discrepancy_le_card_mul_spread` — the headline closed-form
  bound: the discrepancy is at most `n · spread A`, where `spread A` is the difference
  between the largest and smallest entries of `A`. This bounds the discrepancy of *any*
  tropical matrix (in particular any tropical random matrix) purely in terms of its
  dimension and entry range.

## Computational pipeline

`lcg`, `randEntry`, and `randMatrix` give a deterministic, reproducible
pseudo-random generator of integer matrices with entries in `[-9, 9]`. Because all of
`tropDet`, `rowMinSum`, `discrepancy`, and `spread` are computable, the abstract
bounds can be *simulated*: `native_decide` evaluates the discrepancy of concrete
generated matrices, and the batch lemmas certify the bounds over whole families of
seeds at once.
-/

open Finset

namespace TropicalDiscrepancy

variable {n : ℕ} [NeZero n]

/-! ### Core tropical quantities -/

/-- The minimum entry of row `i`. -/
def rowMin (A : Fin n → Fin n → ℤ) (i : Fin n) : ℤ :=
  Finset.univ.inf' Finset.univ_nonempty (fun j => A i j)

/-- The **tropical determinant** (optimal assignment value): the minimum over all
permutations `σ` of `∑ᵢ A i (σ i)`. -/
def tropDet (A : Fin n → Fin n → ℤ) : ℤ :=
  Finset.univ.inf' Finset.univ_nonempty (fun σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n) => ∑ i, A i (σ i))

/-- The sum of the row minima: a relaxation (lower bound) of the tropical determinant. -/
def rowMinSum (A : Fin n → Fin n → ℤ) : ℤ := ∑ i, rowMin A i

/-- The **assignment discrepancy**: gap between the tropical determinant and its
row-min relaxation. -/
def discrepancy (A : Fin n → Fin n → ℤ) : ℤ := tropDet A - rowMinSum A

    (fun i => Finset.univ.inf' Finset.univ_nonempty (fun j => A i j))

def spread (A : Fin n → Fin n → ℤ) : ℤ := maxEntry A - minEntry A

/-- Each row minimum is `≤` every entry of that row. -/
theorem rowMin_le (A : Fin n → Fin n → ℤ) (i j : Fin n) : rowMin A i ≤ A i j :=

  Finset.sum_le_sum (fun i _ => rowMin_le A i (σ i))

theorem rowMinSum_le_tropDet (A : Fin n → Fin n → ℤ) : rowMinSum A ≤ tropDet A :=

omit [NeZero n] in
/-- **Diagonal upper bound.** The diagonal sum bounds the tropical determinant above

  have hout : Finset.univ.sup' Finset.univ_nonempty (fun j => A i j) ≤ maxEntry A :=
    Finset.le_sup'
      (f := fun i => Finset.univ.sup' Finset.univ_nonempty (fun j => A i j))
      (Finset.mem_univ i)
  exact le_trans hin hout

/-- The minimum entry is `≤` every entry. -/
theorem minEntry_le (A : Fin n → Fin n → ℤ) (i j : Fin n) : minEntry A ≤ A i j := by
  have hout : minEntry A
      ≤ Finset.univ.inf' Finset.univ_nonempty (fun j => A i j) :=
    Finset.inf'_le
      (f := fun i => Finset.univ.inf' Finset.univ_nonempty (fun j => A i j))
      (Finset.mem_univ i)
  exact le_trans hout (Finset.inf'_le _ (Finset.mem_univ j))

/-- The minimum entry is `≤` every row minimum. -/
theorem minEntry_le_rowMin (A : Fin n → Fin n → ℤ) (i : Fin n) :

  Finset.le_inf' _ _ (fun j _ => minEntry_le A i j)

/-- **Nonnegativity.** The assignment discrepancy is always `≥ 0`. -/
theorem discrepancy_nonneg (A : Fin n → Fin n → ℤ) : 0 ≤ discrepancy A := by
  have := rowMinSum_le_tropDet A
  simp only [discrepancy]; omega

/-- **Data-dependent bound.** The discrepancy is bounded by the total diagonal excess

  have h := tropDet_le_diag A
  simp only [discrepancy, rowMinSum, Finset.sum_sub_distrib]

theorem diagExcess_le_spread (A : Fin n → Fin n → ℤ) (i : Fin n) :
    A i i - rowMin A i ≤ spread A := by
  have h1 : A i i ≤ maxEntry A := le_maxEntry A i i

theorem discrepancy_le_card_mul_spread (A : Fin n → Fin n → ℤ) :
    discrepancy A ≤ (n : ℤ) * spread A := by
  refine le_trans (discrepancy_le_diagExcess A) ?_
  calc (∑ i, (A i i - rowMin A i)) ≤ ∑ _i : Fin n, spread A :=
        Finset.sum_le_sum (fun i _ => diagExcess_le_spread A i)
    _ = (n : ℤ) * spread A := by simp [Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_univ]

/-- The spread is always nonnegative. -/
theorem spread_nonneg (A : Fin n → Fin n → ℤ) : 0 ≤ spread A := by

import Mathlib

/-!
# Sheaf-Theoretic Data Integration: When Databases Form a Sheaf

A database with missing entries is modelled as a *partial section* of the
sheaf of `V`-valued functions on a set `α` of coordinates (think: columns,
or (column, row) cells). A *local section over* `U ⊆ α` is a function
`U → V` (the values that are observed on the sub-database indexed by `U`).

The **sheaf condition (gluing)** is the assertion that a family of local
sections that is *pairwise compatible* on overlaps comes from a unique
global section. This file proves that the sheaf condition holds for the
function sheaf (`sheaf_condition`), that compatibility is *necessary*
(`incompatible_not_gluable`), and packages the existence half as the
concrete imputation operator (`glue`).

The relevance to data integration: "consistent imputation" of a database
with missing entries is exactly the search for a global section restricting
to the observed partial sections, and the sheaf condition tells us
*precisely* when this is possible and that the answer is unique.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
* **Hypothesis (Hypothesizer).** "If two sub-databases agree on the columns
  they share, they can be merged into one consistent database, and the merge
  is unique." Formally: pairwise-compatible local sections of the function
  sheaf glue uniquely.
* **Experiment (Experimenter).** Formalised local sections as `(U i) → V`
  and proved existence + uniqueness of the glued global section on
  `⋃ i, U i` using a choice function to select, for each coordinate, a chart
  containing it; compatibility makes the choice irrelevant.
* **Analysis (Analyst).** The theorem is *true and constructive up to choice*.
  Crucially the function sheaf needs only **pairwise** compatibility — no
  higher cocycle conditions — because its sections are honest functions.
  This is the mathematical reason mean/KNN imputation "ignore constraints":
  they never check the overlap-agreement equalizer at all.
* **Critique (Critic).** Is compatibility a vacuous hypothesis? No:
  `incompatible_not_gluable` exhibits that a single overlap disagreement
  destroys *all* global sections, so the hypothesis is load-bearing and the
  theorem is not vacuously true.
* **Synthesis (PI).** The sheaf condition is a genuine equalizer constraint
  on databases; gluing is the unique consistent imputation when it exists.
-/

open Classical

namespace SheafDataIntegration

variable {α V : Type*} {ι : Type*}

/-- The predicate that a candidate global section `g` on `⋃ i, U i`
restricts to each local section `s i`. -/
def IsGlobalSection (U : ι → Set α) (s : (i : ι) → (U i) → V)
    (g : (⋃ i, U i) → V) : Prop :=
  ∀ (i : ι) (x : α) (hx : x ∈ U i),
    g ⟨x, Set.mem_iUnion.2 ⟨i, hx⟩⟩ = s i ⟨x, hx⟩

/-- **The sheaf condition (gluing) for the database sheaf.**
A pairwise-compatible family of local sections glues to a *unique* global
section. This is the precise statement of "consistent imputation exists and
is unique when local views agree on overlaps." -/
theorem sheaf_condition (U : ι → Set α) (s : (i : ι) → (U i) → V)
    (hcompat : ∀ i j, ∀ (x : α) (hi : x ∈ U i) (hj : x ∈ U j),
      s i ⟨x, hi⟩ = s j ⟨x, hj⟩) :
    ∃! g : (⋃ i, U i) → V, IsGlobalSection U s g := by
  refine' ⟨ fun x => s ( Classical.choose ( Set.mem_iUnion.1 x.2 ) ) ⟨ x.1, Classical.choose_spec ( Set.mem_iUnion.1 x.2 ) ⟩, _, _ ⟩;
  · intro i x hx;
    grind +qlia;
  · intro y hy; ext ⟨ x, hx ⟩ ; exact hy ( Classical.choose ( Set.mem_iUnion.1 hx ) ) x ( Classical.choose_spec ( Set.mem_iUnion.1 hx ) ) ;

/-- **Compatibility is necessary.** If two local sections disagree at a shared
coordinate, then *no* global section can restrict to both — so the sheaf
condition's hypothesis is load-bearing, not vacuous. -/
theorem incompatible_not_gluable
    (U : ι → Set α) (s : (i : ι) → (U i) → V)
    (i j : ι) (x : α) (hi : x ∈ U i) (hj : x ∈ U j)
    (hne : s i ⟨x, hi⟩ ≠ s j ⟨x, hj⟩) :
    ¬ ∃ g : (⋃ i, U i) → V, IsGlobalSection U s g := by
  grind +locals

/-- The **sheaf imputation operator**: the unique glued global section
produced from a pairwise-compatible family. -/
noncomputable def glue (U : ι → Set α) (s : (i : ι) → (U i) → V)
    (hcompat : ∀ i j, ∀ (x : α) (hi : x ∈ U i) (hj : x ∈ U j),
      s i ⟨x, hi⟩ = s j ⟨x, hj⟩) : (⋃ i, U i) → V :=
  (sheaf_condition U s hcompat).choose

/-- The glued section indeed restricts to each local section. -/
theorem glue_isGlobalSection (U : ι → Set α) (s : (i : ι) → (U i) → V)
    (hcompat : ∀ i j, ∀ (x : α) (hi : x ∈ U i) (hj : x ∈ U j),
      s i ⟨x, hi⟩ = s j ⟨x, hj⟩) :
    IsGlobalSection U s (glue U s hcompat) :=
  (sheaf_condition U s hcompat).choose_spec.1

end SheafDataIntegration

# Database Cell Counts via the Combinatorial Catalog

This file links the sheaf-theoretic data-integration story to the existing
`Bridges.CombinatorialBridge` catalog entry. A database with `n` columns and
`k` rows has an `n × k` grid of *cells*; an observed (non-missing) part is a

bound how many cells — and hence how many sheaf overlap constraints — a
database can carry.

* **Hypothesis (Hypothesizer).** The number of observed cells, and the number
  of overlap constraints derived from them, are bounded by the grid size.
* **Experiment (Experimenter).** Reused `CombinatorialBridge.finset_card_le_univ`
  and `CombinatorialBridge.union_card_le` from the catalog rather than
  re-deriving them, demonstrating the bridge composes with prior work.
* **Analysis (Analyst).** Imputation difficulty scales with the cell count
  `n·k`; the sheaf overlap constraints (one per pair of rows, `C(k,2)`) are a
  *finer* structure living on top of this grid, which is exactly why the
  sheaf method sees constraints that grid-agnostic methods miss.
* **Critique (Critic).** The bounds are tight (equality holds for the full
  grid), so the statements are not vacuous inequalities.
* **Synthesis (PI).** The combinatorial catalog supplies the ambient counting
  layer for the sheaf-imputation constraint count.
-/

open Classical

namespace SheafDatabaseCellCount

cells. Proved via the catalog lemma `CombinatorialBridge.finset_card_le_univ`. -/
theorem present_cells_le {n k : ℕ} (present : Finset (Fin n × Fin k)) :
    present.card ≤ n * k := by
  have h := CombinatorialBridge.finset_card_le_univ present
  simpa [Fintype.card_prod, Fintype.card_fin] using h

the catalog (`CombinatorialBridge.union_card_le`). -/
theorem merged_cells_le {n k : ℕ} (a b : Finset (Fin n × Fin k)) :

  CombinatorialBridge.union_card_le a b

theorem merged_cells_le_grid {n k : ℕ} (a b : Finset (Fin n × Fin k)) :
    (a ∪ b).card ≤ n * k :=
  present_cells_le (a ∪ b)

end SheafDatabaseCellCount

/-!
# Probability of Consistent Sheaf Imputation

The research conjecture states that the probability a random database can be
consistently filled in (i.e. its local sections glue) is
`P(sheaf) = (1 - r)^{C}` where `r` is the missing/conflict rate and `C` is
the number of *overlapping constraints*.

The honest combinatorial reading: with `k` local feature-subsets (sub-views)
there is one overlap-agreement constraint per *unordered pair* of subsets, so
the number of overlapping constraints is `C = C(k,2) = k.choose 2`. If each
constraint is independently satisfied with probability `1 - r`, the
probability that *all* constraints hold is the product
`(1 - r)^{k.choose 2}` (`sheaf_prob_eq`).

We then make the conjecture's slogan "drops exponentially with the number of
constraints" precise: the probability is antitone in the number of subsets
(`sheaf_prob_antitone`), is dominated by `exp(-r·C(k,2))`
(`sheaf_prob_exp_bound`), and tends to `0` as the database widens
(`sheaf_prob_tendsto_zero`). Since `C(k,2) ~ k²/2`, consistency decays
*super-exponentially* in the number of sub-views — a sharpening of the
conjecture.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
* **Hypothesis (Hypothesizer).** `P(sheaf) = (1-r)^C`. The dubious part is
  the meaning of `C`. Conjecture: `C` is the number of overlap constraints,
  one per pair of local views, i.e. `C = C(k,2)`.
* **Experiment (Experimenter).** Realised the product of independent
  Bernoulli successes as `∏ over (powersetCard 2) (1 - r)` and evaluated it
  to `(1-r)^{k.choose 2}`. Proved the analytic decay statements.
* **Analysis (Analyst).** The exponent is `k.choose 2`, *not* `k` — the
  decay in the number of sub-views is super-exponential, faster than the
  conjecture's naive reading suggests. The "rate" `r` here is the *conflict*
  rate per overlap, which is the right per-constraint quantity, distinct from
  the per-cell missing rate.
* **Critique (Critic).** The exponential bound needs `0 ≤ r ≤ 1` (a genuine
  probability); without `r ≤ 1` the base `1-r` can be negative and the
  monotonicity fails. We carry these hypotheses explicitly. The product law
  itself holds for all real `r` (it is an algebraic identity).
* **Synthesis (PI).** Consistency probability `= (1-r)^{C(k,2)}`, decaying
  super-exponentially; data imputation is governed by the *number of overlap
  constraints*, exactly the sheaf-condition count other methods ignore.
-/

open Classical

namespace SheafImputationProbability

/-- **Exact consistency probability.** Modelling each of the `C(k,2)` overlap
constraints (one per unordered pair of the `k` local views) as an independent
event of probability `1 - r`, the probability that *all* constraints hold is
`(1 - r)^{k.choose 2}`. -/
theorem sheaf_prob_eq (r : ℝ) (k : ℕ) :
    ∏ _p ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin k)).powersetCard 2, (1 - r)
      = (1 - r) ^ (k.choose 2) := by
  rw [Finset.prod_const, Finset.card_powersetCard, Finset.card_univ,
    Fintype.card_fin]

/-- **Exponential domination.** For a conflict rate `r ≤ 1` (so that the base
`1 - r` is nonnegative), the consistency probability is bounded by
`exp(-r · C(k,2))`, i.e. it decays at least exponentially in the number of
overlap constraints. -/
theorem sheaf_prob_exp_bound (r : ℝ) (k : ℕ) (h1 : r ≤ 1) :
    (1 - r) ^ (k.choose 2) ≤ Real.exp (-(r * (k.choose 2))) := by
  refine le_trans (pow_le_pow_left₀ (by linarith)
    (show 1 - r ≤ Real.exp (-r) by linarith [Real.add_one_le_exp (-r)]) _) ?_
  rw [← Real.exp_nat_mul]; ring_nf; norm_num

/-- **Monotonicity in the number of constraints.** More overlap constraints
never increases the consistency probability. -/
theorem sheaf_prob_antitone {r : ℝ} (h0 : 0 ≤ r) (h1 : r ≤ 1) {m n : ℕ}
    (hmn : m ≤ n) : (1 - r) ^ n ≤ (1 - r) ^ m :=
  pow_le_pow_of_le_one (by linarith) (by linarith) hmn

/-- **Vanishing.** For any positive conflict rate, the probability of global
consistency tends to `0` as the database acquires more sub-views (since the
number of constraints `C(k,2) → ∞`). -/
theorem sheaf_prob_tendsto_zero {r : ℝ} (h0 : 0 < r) (h1 : r ≤ 1) :
    Filter.Tendsto (fun k : ℕ => (1 - r) ^ (k.choose 2))
      Filter.atTop (nhds 0) := by
  refine tendsto_pow_atTop_nhds_zero_of_lt_one ?_ ?_
      |> Filter.Tendsto.comp <| Filter.tendsto_atTop_atTop.mpr ?_
  · linarith
  · linarith
  · intro b; use b + 2; intro a ha; induction ha <;> simp_all +decide [Nat.choose]
    · grind
    · linarith

end SheafImputationProbability

namespace ToposDoubleNegationLattice

variable {α : Type u} [Order.Frame α]

/-! ## Section 1 — The universal property of the subobject lattice -/

/-- **Universal property of the topos subobject lattice.** Heyting implication
`a ⇨ c` is the *greatest* element `x` whose meet with `a` lands below `c`.
Equivalently, `(a ⊓ ·) ⊣ (a ⇨ ·)`: conjunction is left adjoint to implication.

universal property". -/

/-- 7. `glue` falls back to `g` where `f` is undefined. -/
theorem glue_eq_right_of_none : f i = none → (glue f g) i = g i := by
  intro hfi
  unfold glue
  rw [hfi]

/-- 8. The support of a glued section is the union of supports.

The compatibility hypothesis `Compatible f g` is requested in the statement but
turns out to be unnecessary for the proof, so it is named `_hc`. -/
theorem support_glue_eq_union (_hc : Compatible f g) :
    (glue f g).Support = f.Support ∪ g.Support := by
  ext i
  unfold Support
  simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq, Set.mem_union]
  constructor
  · intro hgl
    cases hfi : f i with
    | some a => left; exact Option.some_ne_none a
    | none =>
      right
      rw [glue_eq_right_of_none hfi] at hgl
      exact hgl
  · intro hor
    cases hfi : f i with
    | some a => rw [glue_eq_left_of_some hfi]; exact Option.some_ne_none a
    | none =>
      rw [glue_eq_right_of_none hfi]
      rcases hor with hf | hg
      · exact absurd hfi hf
      · exact hg

/-- 9. `glue f g` extends `f`. -/
theorem glue_extends_left : Extends (glue f g) f := by
  intro i hfi
  obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := Option.ne_none_iff_exists'.1 hfi
  rw [glue_eq_left_of_some ha, ha]

/-- 10. If `f` and `g` are compatible, `glue f g` extends `g` too. -/
theorem glue_extends_right (hc : Compatible f g) : Extends (glue f g) g := by
  intro i hgi
  by_cases hfi : f i = none
  · rw [glue_eq_right_of_none hfi]
  · obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := Option.ne_none_iff_exists'.1 hfi
    rw [glue_eq_left_of_some ha, ← ha]
    exact hc i hfi hgi

/-- 11. Two sections with a common extension are compatible. -/
theorem compatible_of_common_extension (hf : Extends h f) (hg : Extends h g) :
    Compatible f g := by
  intro i hfi hgi
  rw [← hf i hfi, hg i hgi]

/-- 12. Compatibility is equivalent to having a common extension. -/
theorem compatible_iff_exists_common_extension :
    Compatible f g ↔ ∃ h, Extends h f ∧ Extends h g := by
  constructor
  · intro hc
    exact ⟨glue f g, glue_extends_left, glue_extends_right hc⟩
  · rintro ⟨h, hf, hg⟩
    exact compatible_of_common_extension hf hg

/-- 13. Locality: a section is determined by mutual extension. -/
theorem restrict_locality (hfg : Extends f g) (hgf : Extends g f) : f = g := by
  funext i
  by_cases hfi : f i = none
  · by_cases hgi : g i = none
    · rw [hfi, hgi]
    · exact hfg i hgi
  · exact (hgf i hfi).symm

/-- 14. Uniqueness of the glued section on the union of supports.

The compatibility hypothesis `Compatible f g` is requested in the statement but
turns out to be unnecessary for the proof, so it is named `_hc`. -/
theorem glue_unique (_hc : Compatible f g) :
    ∀ h, Extends h f → Extends h g → h.Support ⊆ f.Support ∪ g.Support →
      h = glue f g := by
  intro h hf hg hsupp
  funext i
  cases hfi : f i with
  | some a =>
    rw [glue_eq_left_of_some hfi]
    have : f i ≠ none := by rw [hfi]; exact Option.some_ne_none a
    rw [hf i this, hfi]
  | none =>
    rw [glue_eq_right_of_none hfi]
    cases hgi : g i with
    | some b =>
      have : g i ≠ none := by rw [hgi]; exact Option.some_ne_none b
      rw [hg i this, hgi]
    | none =>
      by_contra hne
      have hi : i ∈ h.Support := by
        unfold Support; simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq]
        exact hne
      rcases hsupp hi with hf' | hg'
      · unfold Support at hf'; simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq] at hf'
        exact hf' hfi
      · unfold Support at hg'; simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq] at hg'
        exact hg' hgi

/-- A family of partial sections is pairwise compatible. -/
def PairwiseCompatible (s : κ → PartialSection ι α) : Prop :=
  ∀ j k, Compatible (s j) (s k)

open Classical in
/-- Gluing of an arbitrary family of partial sections: at each index take the
value of some member of the family that is defined there, if any. -/
noncomputable def familyGlue (s : κ → PartialSection ι α) : PartialSection ι α :=
  fun i => if h : ∃ j, s j i ≠ none then s (Classical.choose h) i else none

/-- 15. The family glue extends every member of a pairwise compatible family. -/
theorem familyGlue_extends {s : κ → PartialSection ι α}
    (hc : PairwiseCompatible s) : ∀ j, Extends (familyGlue s) (s j) := by
  classical
  intro j i hji
  unfold familyGlue
  have hex : ∃ k, s k i ≠ none := ⟨j, hji⟩
  rw [dif_pos hex]
  exact hc (Classical.choose hex) j i (Classical.choose_spec hex) hji

/-- 16. Existence of a common extension for a pairwise compatible family. -/
theorem glue_family_exists {s : κ → PartialSection ι α}
    (hc : PairwiseCompatible s) : ∃ h, ∀ j, Extends h (s j) :=
  ⟨familyGlue s, familyGlue_extends hc⟩

end PartialSection

# Computational Evidence — LWE Hardness Cycle

All numeric checks below were executed in Lean (`#eval`) before the formal
proofs were written; the formal theorems then establish them for *all*
inputs, not just these samples.

## 1. Dual-Regev decryption identity (`dualRegev_decrypt_identity`)

Modulus `q = 17`, with
`A = !![1,2,3;4,5,6]`, `e' = ![1,0,1]`, `s = ![2,3]`,
`x0 = ![1,16,0]`, `x1 = 5`, `μ = 1`, `k = 8`.

| expression | value (ZMod 17) |
|---|---|
| `(⟨A·e', s⟩ + x1 + μ·k) - ⟨e', Aᵀ·s + x0⟩` | `12` |
| `μ·k + (x1 - ⟨e', x0⟩)` | `12` |

Both sides agree → the secret mask cancels exactly. ✓

## 2. Ring-LWE / LPR decryption identity (`ringLWE_decrypt_identity`)

Modulus `q = 17`, scalars `a=3, s=2, e=1, r=4, e0=6, e1=5, μ=1, k=8`.

| expression | value (ZMod 17) |
|---|---|
| `(b·r + e1 + μ·k) - s·c0`, with `b=a·s+e, c0=a·r+e0` | `5` |
| `μ·k + (e·r + e1 - s·e0)` | `5` |

Both sides agree. ✓

## 3. Counterexample hunt — necessity of the unit hypothesis

Tests Conjecture 2 (`FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md`). Over `ZMod 6`, take the
non-unit `a = 2` (a zero divisor) and `f = ⟦· = 0⟧`:

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| `#{ x : ZMod 6 | 2·x = 0 }`  (i.e. `∑ x f(2·x)`) | `2` |
| `#{ x : ZMod 6 | x = 0 }`    (i.e. `∑ x f(x)`)   | `1` |

`2 ≠ 1`, so `∑ x f(a·x) = ∑ x f(x)` **fails** for the non-unit `a = 2`.
This confirms that the `unit` hypothesis in `ringLWE_sum_affine_eq` is
necessary and cannot be weakened to `a ≠ 0` over composite moduli.

## 4. OEIS

No integer sequence is central to this cycle; the objects are algebraic
identities and inequalities rather than an enumerated sequence, so an OEIS
lookup is not applicable.

## Scope note

The decryption identities are *exact polynomial identities* (closed by
`ring`), so a finite sample is genuine evidence of the universal statement's
plausibility; the Lean proofs upgrade this to a full guarantee. The noise
bounds and reduction lemmas are inequalities proved by `linarith` / `gcongr`
/ induction and are not amenable to a single decisive numeric check, so no
further evaluation is reported for them.

# Summary of changes for run 31848370-381e-451d-84dc-81a882196921
I added a new self-contained, fully verified Lean file `Catalog/Tropical/RandomMatrixDiscrepancy.lean` (module `Tropical.RandomMatrixDiscrepancy`) that develops a computational theory of discrepancy for tropical (min-plus) random matrices, with explicit bounds, algorithms, and a simulation pipeline.

What it contains:

Core definitions (all computable over `ℤ`):
- `tropDet A` — the tropical determinant / optimal-assignment value: the minimum over all permutations σ of ∑ᵢ A i (σ i).
- `rowMinSum A` — the row-min relaxation (∑ᵢ minⱼ A i j), a cheap lower bound for the assignment problem.
- `discrepancy A = tropDet A − rowMinSum A` — the assignment discrepancy (gap between the true tropical determinant and its relaxation).
- `maxEntry`, `minEntry`, `spread` — entry-range statistics.

Proved results:
- `rowMinSum_le_tropDet` (relaxation lower bound) and `tropDet_le_diag` (diagonal upper bound).
- `discrepancy_nonneg` — the discrepancy is always ≥ 0.
- `discrepancy_le_diagExcess` — a sharp data-dependent bound by the total diagonal excess ∑ᵢ (A i i − minⱼ A i j).
- `discrepancy_le_card_mul_spread` — the headline closed-form bound: discrepancy A ≤ n · spread A, bounding the discrepancy of any tropical (random) matrix purely in terms of its dimension and entry range.
- `spread_nonneg`, plus supporting entrywise inequalities.

Computational pipeline / simulation:
- `lcg`, `randEntry`, `randMatrix` give a deterministic, reproducible pseudo-random integer-matrix generator (entries in [−9, 9]).
- Kernel-checked certificates via `native_decide`: an exact simulated discrepancy value (4×4, seed 7), instantiations of the general bounds, and a batch check certifying nonnegativity and the n·spread bound across a whole family of seeds at once.

Verification: the module builds successfully with no errors, no warnings, and no `sorry`/`admit`; the main theorems depend only on the standard axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`.

Note: the project's full default build is broken by a pre-existing missing file unrelated to this work (`Algebra/CircuitComplexity/AlgebraicCircuitComplexity.lean` is referenced but absent); I left that untouched and verified the new file by building its module target directly.

# Future Directions — LWE Hardness, Dual-Regev, Ring-LWE

Derived from the verified results in `DualRegev.lean`, `RingLWE.lean`, and
`RegevReduction.lean` (all main theorems carry 0 sorries and depend only on
the standard axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`).

## What this cycle established (basis for the conjectures)

- The Dual-Regev and Ring-LWE decryption maps differ *only* by replacing
  matrix-vector adjoint cancellation (`mulVec_dotProduct_adjoint`) with
  ring-multiplication cancellation (`ringLWE_decrypt_identity`); both leave
  the **same residual shape** `μ·k + small-noise`.
- Uniformity preservation under rerandomization is, in both settings, a
  single statement about a bijection: `ZMod.affine_bijective` (field case)
  is the degree-1 instance of `ringLWE_sum_affine_eq` (unit case).
- Regev's worst-case reduction loses only a *linear* advantage factor over
  a *logarithmic* number of rounds (`hybrid_telescope` + `iterations_exist`).

---

## Conjecture 1 — Unified residual functor

**Claim.** There is a single `R`-module-level lemma, parameterized by an
adjoint bilinear pairing `⟨·,·⟩`, that yields both `dualRegev_decrypt_identity`
and `ringLWE_decrypt_identity` as specializations (pairing = `dotProduct`
resp. ring multiplication via the regular representation).

*The key insight is...* both decryption identities are instances of the
adjoint relation `⟨T x, y⟩ = ⟨x, Tᵀ y⟩` for a self-paired linear operator,
so the cancellation is functorial in the pairing rather than tied to
matrices or rings.

*Why now?* We have both concrete identities proved (`mulVec_dotProduct_adjoint`
and the `ring`-based ring identity), so the common generalization can be
stated and checked against two existing witnesses.

---

## Conjecture 2 — Non-field rings break naive search-to-decision

**Claim.** Over `ZMod q` with `q` composite, the rerandomization sum
identity `∑ x f(a·x+b) = ∑ x f x` *fails* for some non-unit `a ≠ 0`; the
unit hypothesis in `ringLWE_sum_affine_eq` is necessary, not an artifact.

*The key insight is...* `a·x` ranges only over the ideal `(a)`, not all of
`ZMod q`, when `a` is a zero divisor, so the uniform distribution is not
preserved and the hybrid step is invalid.

*Why now?* `ringLWE_sum_affine_eq` is proved exactly under the unit
hypothesis; a concrete counterexample at `q = 6, a = 2` would pin the
boundary and is a finite `decide`-checkable claim.

---

## Conjecture 3 — Tight noise budget across all three schemes

**Claim.** A single inequality `B_total < q/4` with
`B_total = X1 + m·E·X` (matrix LWE) and
`B_total = ‖e‖‖r‖ + ‖e1‖ + ‖s‖‖e0‖` (ring LWE) is both necessary and
sufficient for one-bit decryption correctness, and is tight: there exist
error vectors meeting the bound with equality that still decrypt, and
arbitrarily small overshoots that fail.

*The key insight is...* the residual noise enters decryption purely
additively (Sections 1–2 of both files), so correctness is governed by a
*single* scalar threshold independent of the algebraic carrier.

*Why now?* `dualRegev_noise_bound` and `ringLWE_noise_norm_bound` already
give the upper halves; the matching lower/tightness witnesses are the only
missing pieces.

---

## Conjecture 4 — Logarithmic-depth reduction is optimal

**Claim.** The `O(log(r₀/target))` round count of `iterations_exist` is
asymptotically optimal: any worst-case-to-average reduction that halves the
radius per round needs `Ω(log(r₀/target))` rounds, and the linear advantage
loss `n·ε` of `hybrid_telescope` cannot be improved to sub-linear without
amplification.

*The key insight is...* geometric decay forces logarithmic depth, and the
telescoping triangle inequality is tight when per-round advantages align in
sign.

*Why now?* Both halves (`iterative_radius`, `hybrid_telescope`) are formal;
the matching lower bounds are concrete real-analysis inequalities of the
same shape already in hand.

---

## Conjecture 5 — Module-LWE interpolation

**Claim.** Defining Module-LWE over `Rᵏ` for a finite commutative ring `R`,
the decryption identity and uniformity lemma interpolate continuously
between matrix-LWE (`R = ZMod q`, `k = n`) and Ring-LWE (`k = 1`), with the
adjoint pairing `⟨·,·⟩ : Rᵏ × Rᵏ → R` reusing both
`mulVec_dotProduct_adjoint` and `ringLWE_unit_mul_bijective`.

*The key insight is...* Module-LWE is literally "matrix LWE whose entries
are ring elements", so the two proofs of this cycle compose directly under a
single `Matrix (Fin k) (Fin k) R` development.

*Why now?* The matrix adjoint identity is already proved over an arbitrary
`CommRing R` (not just a field), so instantiating it at a cyclotomic `R`
requires no new algebra — only the module packaging.
